title: 400 YOUNG WOMEN WERE TAKEN FROM THEIR HOMES AND GIVEN TO 400 MEN—AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART IS THAT ISRAEL THOUGHT IT WAS DOING THE RIGHT THING
paragraphs: 400 YOUNG WOMEN WERE TAKEN FROM THEIR HOMES AND GIVEN TO 400 MEN—AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART IS THAT ISRAEL THOUGHT IT WAS DOING THE RIGHT THING

An almost forgotten tragedy in Judges 21 exposes what happens when people use religion to justify cruelty, when innocent lives become solutions to someone else's mistakes, and why a broken world desperately needs the grace and kingship of Jesus Christ.
“And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young virgins... and they brought them unto the camp to Shiloh.” — Judges 21:12, KJV
Imagine being a young woman in a quiet town.
You know the streets. You recognize the voices outside your home. You have people you love, perhaps dreams you have never told anyone about, and a future you believe is still yours to live.
Then one day, armed men arrive.
Not strangers from a foreign nation.
Men from your own people.
Men who speak the language of your ancestors. Men who know the name of the God your nation worships.
And by the time the violence ends, your community has been devastated.
Your father may be dead.
Your mother may be dead.
Your brothers may be dead.
The home that once sheltered you may be gone.
And somehow, after everything you have suffered, the men responsible for the destruction decide that your future belongs to somebody else.
You are not asked what you want.
You are not given time to grieve.
You are not invited to choose.
You are counted.
One among four hundred.
Then handed over to a man whose name you may never have heard.
And the people arranging it believe they have found a solution.
This is not a fictional horror story.
This is one of the most disturbing accounts preserved in the Bible.
Judges 21:10–14.
Four hundred young women from Jabesh-gilead were taken and given to the surviving men of Benjamin.
But here is the question that should trouble every person who has ever opened a Bible:
How did a nation that belonged to God become capable of doing something so terrible while believing it was repairing what had gone wrong?
And an even more uncomfortable question follows.
What happens when we become so determined to fix our mistakes that we stop seeing the people we are hurting?
Stay with this account.
Because the greatest danger in Judges 21 is not merely the violence that happened thousands of years ago.
It is the frightening possibility that human beings can become so convinced of their own righteousness that they no longer recognize their cruelty.
And by the end, we will discover why this terrible chapter does not invite us to admire Israel's solution.
It makes us long for a better King.
A King whose name is Jesus.
Before we reach those four hundred women, we need to understand how Israel arrived at this terrible moment.
The story begins with another woman.
An unnamed concubine.

Judges 19 records how she suffered horrific abuse in the town of Gibeah, within the territory of Benjamin. After her death, her body was dismembered and its parts sent throughout Israel, provoking national outrage.
The chapter is difficult to read.
It should be.
Scripture does not preserve every terrible event because God approves of it.
Sometimes Scripture exposes the depths of human evil so that we will understand just how desperately humanity needs redemption.
Israel was horrified by the crime committed at Gibeah.
And rightly so.
But what followed was not a simple story of justice triumphing over wickedness.
The tribe of Benjamin refused to surrender the guilty men, and civil war erupted.
Israel fought against Benjamin.
Thousands died.
Cities were destroyed.
And eventually, according to Judges 20:47, only six hundred Benjaminite men escaped to the rock of Rimmon.
Six hundred survivors.
An entire tribe was approaching extinction.
The Israelites suddenly realized what they had done.
They had been outraged by wickedness, but their response had contributed to a national catastrophe.
And now they were grieving.
Judges 21:2–3 describes the people gathering at Bethel, weeping before God, and asking why one tribe should be missing from Israel.
It sounds like repentance.
It sounds like spiritual sorrow.
But sorrow and repentance are not always the same thing.
A person can weep over consequences without truly confronting the heart that produced them.
A community can regret a disaster while continuing to think in the same destructive ways that created it.
And that is exactly what makes the next part so frightening.
The Israelites had sworn that none of them would give a daughter in marriage to Benjamin.
Now they wanted to preserve the tribe.
But they also wanted to keep their oath.
Instead of humbly confronting the moral disaster before them, they searched for a way around their predicament.
They remembered another oath involving those who had failed to assemble before the LORD at Mizpah.
When they discovered that Jabesh-gilead had not attended, they decided to punish the city.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable.

Judges 21:10–11 says that the congregation sent twelve thousand fighting men against Jabesh-gilead with instructions to kill its inhabitants, except for young women who had not had sexual relations with a man.
Then comes verse 12.
Four hundred young women were found.
They were brought to the camp at Shiloh.
And verse 14 records that they were given to the surviving Benjamites.
The Hebrew text is especially revealing.
Judges 21:12 uses the expression:
אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת נַעֲרָה בְתוּלָה
Arba me'ot na'arah vetulah.
In context, this means four hundred young virgin women.
The word na'arah refers to a girl or young woman. Betulah commonly denotes a virgin, and the surrounding Hebrew wording explicitly identifies these women as having had no sexual relations with a man.
These are not four hundred volunteers stepping forward to rebuild a devastated tribe.
The narrative describes women selected after a military assault.
Then Judges 21:14 says:
וַיִּתְּנוּ לָהֶם הַנָּשִׁים
Vayyittenu lahem hannashim.
Meaning:
“And they gave them the women.”
That is the language of the narrative.
They gave them the women.
Not, “The women chose husbands.”
Not, “The women freely agreed.”
Not, “The women were consulted.”
The text does not record their consent.
It does not preserve their individual names.
It does not tell us what happened when they realized they would be separated from their former lives and given to the surviving men of Benjamin.
We should not invent conversations or details that Scripture does not supply.
But neither should we pretend that silence means consent.
The passage describes the women being taken in the aftermath of violence and transferred to men as part of a tribal survival plan.
The men saw four hundred solutions. But there were four hundred human lives.
Four hundred people whose suffering mattered.
Four hundred people whose dignity did not disappear because powerful men were trying to solve a national crisis.
And perhaps that is what makes this chapter so painful.
The Israelites were trying to preserve a tribe.
But in doing so, they inflicted devastation upon another community.
They wanted to repair what war had broken.
Yet their solution created more victims.
They wanted to keep their vows.
Yet they failed to reckon adequately with the human cost of their decisions.
And here is something we must understand if we want to read the Bible faithfully.
Just because an action is recorded in Scripture does not mean that God commanded it, approved it, or intended it as an example for His people to follow.
The Bible is not merely a collection of admirable people making admirable decisions.
It is also the truthful record of humanity's sin, rebellion, self-deception, and desperate need for divine mercy.
In fact, Judges gives us its own interpretive warning.
The book ends with these words:
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.” — Judges 21:25, KJV
In Hebrew, the final phrase reads:
אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Ish hayyashar be'enav ya'aseh.
The sense is that each person did what was right in his own eyes.
Notice the problem.
They were not necessarily doing what they believed was evil.
They were doing what seemed right to them.
And that is a far more dangerous spiritual condition than many of us realize.
Because a person who knows he is doing wrong may still be confronted by his conscience.
But a person who has convinced himself that his wrongdoing is righteous can become frighteningly difficult to correct.
He can wound people and call it discipline.
He can control people and call it protection.
He can humiliate people and call it correction.
He can demand silence and call it unity.
He can use the language of God while ignoring the character of God.
And sometimes, the people most deeply wounded are the very people who trusted that spiritual language.
Perhaps you understand that pain.
Maybe you have never stood in ancient Jabesh-gilead.
But you know what it feels like when someone else makes a decision and expects you to carry the consequences.
You know what it feels like to have your voice dismissed.
To be told that your pain is inconvenient.
To hear someone explain why the harm they caused was necessary.
Perhaps someone used religion to make you feel guilty for speaking about what happened.
Perhaps you were told to forgive before anyone was willing to acknowledge the truth.
Perhaps you were pressured to remain silent because exposing wrongdoing might embarrass a family, a ministry, or a community.
And somewhere along the way, you began to wonder whether God cared about the things nobody else seemed willing to see.
Listen carefully.
God's Word does not require us to call evil good simply because religious people committed it.
Isaiah 5:20 warns against calling evil good and good evil.
Micah 6:8 calls God's people to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him.
Psalm 34:18 declares that the LORD is near to the brokenhearted.
And Jesus Himself confronted religious leaders who placed heavy burdens on others while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
Matthew 23:23.
That matters.
Because the God revealed in Scripture is not honored when His name is used to excuse cruelty.
He is honored when His truth exposes sin and His grace leads people toward repentance.
There is another detail in Judges 21 that makes the entire tragedy even more revealing.
Four hundred women were not enough.
There were six hundred surviving Benjaminite men.
After the women from Jabesh-gilead were given to them, two hundred men still had no wives.
So the leaders devised another plan.
Judges 21:19–23 describes a festival at Shiloh where the remaining Benjamites were instructed to seize young women who came out to dance.
The men did so.
And the chapter moves toward its haunting conclusion.
Think about that.
The attempt to solve one moral catastrophe led to another.
And then another.
The leaders were so focused on preserving their tribe and navigating their vows that women repeatedly became the means by which the crisis would be resolved.
This is what happens when human beings try to manage sin without surrendering to God's righteousness.
We do not heal evil by giving it a more acceptable explanation.
We do not restore what is broken by making innocent people pay the price.
And we do not become righteous merely because our intentions sound noble.
Proverbs 14:12 warns:
“There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.” — KJV
How many families have been wounded by someone who insisted, “I only wanted what was best”?
How many relationships have collapsed because somebody was more committed to being right than to being truthful?
How many churches have damaged trust because protecting appearances became more important than protecting people?
How many of us have justified our own behavior by focusing on our intentions instead of facing its impact?
That last question is especially uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to condemn the men of Judges 21.
It is harder to recognize the smaller versions of their reasoning in ourselves.
When we refuse to apologize because we believe our motives were good.
When we manipulate a situation because we think the outcome will be beneficial.
When we make promises rashly and then hurt other people rather than humbly admitting we were wrong.
When we sacrifice compassion to protect our pride.
When we demand that others carry burdens we created.
And when we use spiritual language to avoid spiritual accountability.
The distance between ancient Israel and the modern human heart is not as great as we might wish.
That is why this chapter should lead us beyond outrage.
It should lead us toward examination.
Toward humility.
Toward repentance.
Because the problem beneath the violence in Judges was not simply a lack of organization.
It was the deeper corruption of human hearts that needed the righteous rule of God.
And here is where the Gospel changes everything.
The final words of Judges tell us there was no king in Israel.
But the Bible does not end there.
The story continues through Israel's kings, its prophets, its failures, its exile, and its longing for the promised Messiah.
And eventually, a King arrives.
Not merely another ruler with a crown.
Not another powerful man willing to sacrifice the weak for his own survival.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God.
The promised Son of David.
The righteous King.
And look at how differently He treats people.
In John 4, Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman whose personal history had become complicated and painful.
He does not reduce her to a scandal.
He speaks truthfully with her and reveals Himself as the Messiah.
In John 8, Jesus refuses to participate in the hypocritical condemnation of a woman brought before Him, while still calling her away from sin.
In Luke 7, a woman known publicly as sinful approaches Jesus in tears.
Others see her reputation.
Jesus recognizes her faith and speaks of forgiveness.
In Mark 5, a woman who has suffered from bleeding for twelve years reaches for His garment.
She is not merely another interruption in a crowded day.
Jesus stops.
He listens.
He calls her daughter.
And in John 20, Mary Magdalene encounters the risen Christ, who calls her by name and sends her to tell the disciples what she has witnessed.
Do you see the difference?
In Judges 21, four hundred women are counted and distributed.
In the Gospels, Jesus repeatedly demonstrates that people overlooked, shamed, or dismissed by society are not invisible to Him.
He sees.
He listens.
He tells the truth.
He calls people to repentance.
He restores dignity.
And He offers something no human system can manufacture.
Redemption.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus does not simply arrive to make wounded people feel better.
He comes to deal with the deepest problem beneath all human wickedness.
Sin.
The rebellion that distorts our desires.
The pride that convinces us we are righteous while we harm others.
The selfishness that makes other people expendable.
The guilt we cannot erase by explaining ourselves.
The shame we cannot heal by pretending nothing happened.
And the separation from God that none of us can overcome by our own goodness.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — KJV
That includes the people who wound others.
And it includes every one of us who needs God's mercy.
But Romans 5:8 gives us the astonishing answer:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to give humanity better religious language.
He came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He suffered under human injustice.
He was falsely accused, mocked, condemned, and crucified.
And at the cross, He willingly gave His life for our sins.
Not because evil had become good.
Not because injustice no longer mattered.
But because God is both righteous and merciful.
Jesus bore the judgment sinners deserve so that all who trust in Him may receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
And on the third day, He rose from the dead.
The resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word.
Now listen to the astonishing contrast.
In Judges 21, innocent people were made to bear the consequences of decisions made by powerful men.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God willingly offered Himself to save the guilty.
These are not morally equivalent events.
The women of Jabesh-gilead were not presented in Scripture as willing sacrifices, and their suffering should never be romanticized as a picture of the cross.
The contrast is precisely what reveals the difference between human exploitation and divine love.
Human sin takes from the vulnerable. Christ freely gives Himself for sinners.
Jesus says in John 10:18 that no one takes His life from Him; He lays it down of His own accord.
That is not coercion.
That is willing, sacrificial love.
And through His death and resurrection, Jesus opens the way for broken sinners to be forgiven, changed, and brought into the family of God.
This is why the Gospel is not simply about escaping the consequences of our actions.
It is about becoming new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις, kainē ktisis, means new creation.
Not merely a polished version of the old self.
Not a better public image.
Not a religious mask placed over an unchanged heart.
New creation.
A life transformed through union with Jesus Christ.
And that transformation has consequences.
The person who once manipulated others must learn truthfulness.
The person who once excused cruelty must learn repentance.
The person who once demanded forgiveness without accountability must learn humility.
The person who once treated others as disposable must learn to recognize their God-given dignity.
And the person who has been wounded must never be told that following Jesus requires pretending the wound was harmless.
Biblical forgiveness is not the same as denying wrongdoing.
Grace does not require calling abuse love.
Reconciliation is not the same as ignoring danger.
And repentance is not merely saying sorry because consequences have arrived.
Real repentance involves turning from sin toward God, with a changed life that bears fruit consistent with that turning.
Jesus says in Luke 13:3:
“Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.” — KJV
The Greek verb μετανοῆτε, metanoēte, expresses the call to repent.
It is not simply an invitation to feel regret.
It calls for a genuine turning of heart and life.
And that is where this ancient story becomes deeply personal.
Because perhaps you are reading this as someone who has been hurt.
Or perhaps you are reading it as someone who has hurt others.
Maybe both are true.
Maybe you have spent years carrying wounds that nobody acknowledged.
Maybe you have been living with the consequences of someone else's choices.
Maybe you have wondered whether God could ever restore the parts of your life that were taken from you.
Or maybe the Holy Spirit is bringing something else to your attention.
A conversation where you were cruel.
A person you controlled.
A promise you used as an excuse.
A relationship you damaged.
A truth you buried because admitting it would cost you your reputation.
And suddenly this story is no longer about four hundred women in an ancient city.
It is about the human heart standing before a holy God.
What will you do when His Word exposes you?
Will you defend yourself?
Will you explain away the damage?
Will you hide behind your intentions?
Or will you come to Jesus?
Not with a performance.
Not with a religious speech.
Not with excuses.
But with the truth.
“Lord, I have sinned.”
“Lord, I have been wounded.”
“Lord, I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I need Your mercy.”
There is no shame in bringing the truth into the presence of the Savior.
The shame is in loving darkness so much that we refuse the light.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
And for the wounded person who has wondered whether God sees what happened, remember this:
The Bible did not erase the tragedy at Jabesh-gilead.
It preserved the account.
Not every victim is named.
Not every question is answered.
Not every earthly injustice is resolved within the pages of the narrative.
But Scripture refuses to pretend that Israel's darkest failures never happened.
And the wider testimony of God's Word assures us that the Lord is righteous, that He sees oppression, and that He will ultimately judge evil.
Revelation 21:4 promises a coming day when God will wipe away every tear and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise does not make present suffering insignificant.
It means suffering will not have the final word.
And for those who belong to Jesus Christ, there is a future that human cruelty cannot cancel.
A resurrection hope.
A righteous King.
A kingdom where justice is not sacrificed to convenience.
A kingdom where evil cannot disguise itself forever.
A kingdom where the Lamb who was slain reigns.
This is why we cannot end Judges 21 by saying, “What a terrible story,” and simply close our Bibles.
We must ask what kind of King we are following.
Are we following the king of our own opinions?
The king of our pride?
The king of our public reputation?
The king of whatever seems right in our own eyes?
Or are we following Jesus?
Because it is possible to be surrounded by religious activity and still resist the rule of Christ.
It is possible to know Bible verses and refuse correction.
It is possible to defend truth loudly while failing to practice mercy.
It is possible to speak about holiness while treating people as though they have no dignity.
And it is possible to build something that looks spiritually impressive while neglecting the very character of the Savior we claim to represent.
Jesus did not call us to build reputations for ourselves.
He called us to follow Him.
To deny ourselves.
To take up our cross.
To love one another.
To proclaim the Gospel.
To make disciples.
To teach obedience to everything He commanded.
And that brings us to something I want to ask you personally.
If this account has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past that conviction.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to seek forgiveness, seek it.
If you need to stop justifying harmful behavior, stop.
If you need to tell the truth about something you have endured, know that seeking appropriate help, protection, and wise counsel is not a failure of faith.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not mistake knowing religious stories for knowing the Savior.
Come to Him in faith.
Believe that He died for your sins and rose again.
Turn from sin.
Trust in His grace.
Follow Him as Lord.
You do not have to manufacture your own salvation.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast.
No donation can earn it.
No religious achievement can replace it.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And He is enough.
But when His grace changes our hearts, it also changes what we choose to support, share, and build.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to make the darkness more sensational.
Not to exploit the pain of people in Scripture.
Not to turn conviction into entertainment.
But to keep pointing wounded, wandering, searching, and spiritually hungry people back to the living Word of God and the saving Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Every article is an opportunity to open Scripture.
Every testimony is an opportunity to remember His mercy.
Every devotional is an opportunity to grow deeper in truth.
And every person who discovers the Gospel may become someone who carries that message into another life.
These resources are meant to encourage biblical understanding, strengthen faith, nourish discipleship, and help believers continue walking with Christ long after they finish reading a single article.
And if these writings have helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, find encouragement, or draw nearer to Jesus, I want to invite you to become part of sustaining and expanding this work.
Your generosity should never come from pressure, fear, or the belief that God will love you more if you pay.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You can still pray.
You can still read.
You can still grow.
You can still share the truth.
The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is helping more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
It is making room for someone else to discover the grace that has been transforming your own life.
And please do not underestimate what sharing this article can do.
Not because every person will agree with it.
Not because everyone will understand it immediately.
Someone may need to discover that the Bible itself exposes religious corruption.
Someone may need to understand that Jesus does not excuse sin merely because it wears a spiritual disguise.
Someone may be struggling with guilt, wondering whether repentance is still possible.
Someone may be carrying a wound they have never been able to explain.
And someone may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from turning toward Christ.
Bring the person who is hungry for God's Word.
Bring the believer who is struggling.
Bring the person who has grown spiritually cold.
Bring the skeptic who has difficult questions.
Bring the friend who is searching for truth.
Not because we have all the answers.
But because we can keep opening the Scriptures together and pointing one another to the One who is the way, the truth, and the life.
And before you leave, I want to ask you to do something more personal than simply reacting to this article.
Not to impress anybody.
Not to pretend you have everything figured out.
But because honest words can become the beginning of a meaningful conversation.
If you are tired of hiding behind a strong appearance while struggling inside, you can simply write:
And if you have experienced the transforming mercy of Jesus Christ, share a little of your testimony. You never know who may find courage in hearing how God has been at work in your life.
You do not need to disclose private trauma or personal details to prove your faith.
Sometimes the most meaningful testimony is a simple, honest sentence.
“I am still learning to trust Jesus.”
“I need His forgiveness.”
“I am still healing.”
“God has not given up on me.”
Because the Gospel is not the story of perfect people congratulating themselves.
It is the good news of a perfect Savior rescuing sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And now, return with me one last time to Jabesh-gilead.
Four hundred young women.
Four hundred lives altered by the decisions of others.
Four hundred names the biblical account does not preserve.
We do not know how each woman's story unfolded.
We are not told whether any of them later experienced safety, kindness, or restoration.
The text does not give us permission to invent a happy ending.
And we should not.
Some biblical accounts are meant to leave us deeply unsettled.
Some chapters expose wounds that no human explanation can neatly close.
But the silence surrounding these women does not make their suffering meaningless.
It confronts us with the failure of human righteousness when people abandon the justice and mercy of God.
And it leaves us longing for the King who never confuses exploitation with love.
The King who does not need to hide the truth.
The King who does not save His reputation by sacrificing the vulnerable.
The King who willingly laid down His own life for sinners.
The King who rose again.
The King who will return in righteousness.
Jesus Christ.
So when you remember Judges 21, do not remember only the number four hundred.
Remember the danger of a heart that refuses correction.
Remember the cost of trying to repair sin through further wrongdoing.
Remember that the Bible's honesty about human evil is not God's endorsement of that evil.
Remember that religious language cannot make injustice holy.
And above all, remember that the final answer to humanity's brokenness is not our ability to make everything seem right in our own eyes.
It is surrender to the righteous and merciful King.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who forgives those who come to Him in faith.
The One who transforms hearts through His grace.
The One whose kingdom will finally make all things new.
The world may forget the names of those it wounded, but no life is beyond the sight of the King who wore a crown of thorns.
